text: Adolfo Alsina Maza (January 4, 1829 – December 29, 1877) was an Argentine lawyer and Unitarian politician, one of the founders of the Autonomist Party and the National Autonomist Party. Born in Buenos Aires, he was the son of Unitarian politician Valentín Alsina and Antonia Maza, daughter of Manuel Vicente Maza. When Juan Manuel de Rosas became Governor of Buenos Aires Province for the second time in 1835, Alsina moved to Montevideo, Uruguay, where he began his law studies. After the Battle of Caseros in 1852, his family returned to Argentina, and his father was appointed Minister by President Vicente López y Planes. Alsina completed law school and joined the Unitarian army during the civil war. In 1860, following the Battle of Pavón and the National Union Pact, he participated in the commission responsible for the 1860 constitution reform and was elected a deputy in 1862. When federalisation, supported by Bartolomé Mitre, was discussed in the Chamber of Deputies, Alsina caused a split in the Partido Unitario and founded the Partido Autonomista. In 1866, he was elected governor of the Buenos Aires Province; although he considered running for president, he withdrew after realizing he lacked support from most of the province. Domingo Sarmiento was elected president and named Alsina his vice-president. Upon Sarmiento’s presidency ending in 1874, Alsina joined Nicolás Avellaneda to establish the Partido Autonomista Nacional, through which Avellaneda became president and appointed Alsina Minister of War and Navy. In late 1875, Native Americans of Patagonia and the Pampas, particularly the Mapuche, launched organized resistance against the expansion of the nation’s southern border, marking the beginning of the "Conquest of the Desert." The first phase involved the construction of a two-meter deep, three-meter wide trench known as the zanja de Alsina to block the movement of horses and stolen cattle. Alsina also ordered the building of interconnected forts linked by telegraph. Seeking to understand the native peoples, he personally studied the situation but fell ill in the Pampas town of Carhué and died of renal failure at the age of 48.
